en: Evil intent showed in his eyes,
Evasion lay in his words.
He meant to strike me down if he could.
Malice showed in his eyes;
Finding his chance in this way,
That Kalmyk meant to finish me!
Pouring spirits into his barrel,
Deceiving your father and making him drunk,
Thus that Chinese brought me to ruin!
His champions of every sort
Thrust spears through the smoke.
His warriors clad in mail of iron cords,
His dagger-handed men,
His marksmen who never missed,
His heroes drawing bows,
The Chinese all came swarming.
I, your unfortunate mother,
Continued to bear their torment.
They drew bows, making arrows rain,
Fired shot like hail,
The black-burning shot flashed thick,
My misery boiled, with no support to be found.
It was like a deep-dug hollow, a pit,
So much misery set to boil.
When the Kalmyks inflicted their violence,
Your dear, fierce mother—
When they surrounded her,
Akayar, who could lift a camel,
Your father's mighty wrestler,
Seized your father, huge as Opol-Too,
Before a word could be uttered,
In the blink of an eye,
And reached me faster than an arrow.
“Sister-in-law, fierce one, flee!” he said.
“Your accomplished Sultan Manas—
Let me reach you and entrust him to you!
Resourceful sister-in-law Kanykei,
For your generous Sultan Manas
Find some means of rescue,” he said.
“Oh, my sister-in-law Kanykei,
Ride to some place of safety!”
“If you let the reeling lord
Fall, disgrace will be yours.
My peerless, resourceful one,
I entrust my generous lord to you!
What woman could equal you?
Who could call you merely a woman and prosper?
Do not let the faithless dogs torment him:
Grasp him round the waist and carry him away.
My valiant sister-in-law Kanykei,
Take this Manas here—
Carry his bones to Mecca!
Noble sister-in-law Kanykei,
Dedicate Ak-kula to him and slaughter him.
Conceal the generous lord's face;
Lay him in a place blessed by ancestral spirits.
Cross beyond the broad reaches of Kyrym.
Thus have we lost our valiant lord!
Sister-in-law, flee toward Mecca!
Shoot a wild sheep and eat as you go.
Alone in battle, with no companion,
Say that Akayar has died.
If you lose him, disgrace will be yours.
Farewell, sister-in-law Kanykei,
I entrust my fierce lord to you!
Tell the warriors, tell your khan;
When you reach Mecca, sister-in-law,
Tell all the renowned people of Islam!
Tell the khojas in striped robes,
Tell the mullahs in white turbans,
Tell the wise old men;
If you reach them alive, sister-in-law,
Tell all those people!
God knows whether we shall die.
God knows whether the fierce lord
We shall return to see alive.
My leopard-hearted sister-in-law Kanykei,
You gathered forty companions and lived long with them.
Together with your fierce lord,
You called the Kalmyks your kin.
My valiant sister-in-law, farewell!
Your bountiful churning vessel—
Now, sister-in-law, do you see?
Your five Kalmyks have brought you to ruin!
Farewell, sister-in-law; mark this:
The five Kalmyks have churned your milk-skin!
They have eaten your well-nourished foal.
They set themselves up as Manas's equals,
Claiming to be brothers of his own blood.
They studied your tales and songs.
Your Kalmyks who came from Beijing
Studied and learned your secrets.
Drunk on liquor, they ran wild;
In their frenzy they wrecked your camp.
Your Kalmyk kinsmen are your enemies.
It is true, sister-in-law Kanykei:
Your sorrow remains within you.
The pass road runs through Kara-Kyya.
I have entrusted your fierce lord to you.
My leopard-hearted sister-in-law, farewell!”
Speaking at length, Akayar,
With the lord barely alive,
Delivered the gray-maned hero to me.
His fine mustache drooped.
Stricken by a terrible sickness,
As though departing for Judgment Day,
At times he could speak,
At times he could not.
In desperate haste, I, the fierce woman,
Clasped the generous lord tightly,
Laid him crosswise before me,
And settled him on the white saddle.
Beneath me was the tulpar Ak-kula.
The swift steed, in splendid flesh,
I lashed wildly with my whip,
Spurring him on either side.
Shrieking, invoking the true God,
I gathered his reins firmly.
Sobbing, invoking the true God,
I hurried beyond all reason,
Unable to collect my wits.
Bek-Zhailoo at the head of Besh-Tash—
Toward Bek-Zhailoo I fled.
As I made my escape,
Kokchokoz and Kozkaman
Drew their bows like pouring rain,
Shot their missiles like hail.
Kozkaman's marksman,
In that cruel battle, that great turmoil,
With the twelve-charge Ochogor,
At your fierce, ruin-bringing mother
Fired twelve times in succession.
When the shot came, disaster struck:
It tore a wound in my breast.
The lacquered arrow with golden ears,
While your poor father lay intoxicated,
Brought your mother terrible trouble.
A black night descended on me.
There was no one to stand by me.
Such a day of hardship befell me!
There was no forest to flee into,
I had no strength to rely on,
No place to hide.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow:
Such is this shitty world!
On one side, aching and throbbing,
The very core of my heart—
Your father, the generous leopard and lion—
Hovered between life and death.
The missile shattered my flesh
Beneath my right breast.
As I fled carrying your father,
By Kozkaman's shot
My breast was torn away.
Pallid as a grieving widow,
All my body and head
Streamed with sweat down to my feet.
The earth broke into dust.
I, your mother Kanykei,
Was red with blood like a blood-filled skin.
Barely escaping death,
With the vicious slaves from China,
Those villains, I fought.
Dust rose and choked my throat.
Carrying your lion-hearted father before me,
I lost blood and strength.
The wide world closed in on me.
Saliva sweeter than sugar—
I yearned for a single swallow.
When I carried your father away,
For seven days I journeyed on,
Wounded through and through.
For nine days I pressed on,
Covered all over in wounds.
Enduring grievous torment,
I lost consciousness entirely,
My breast torn open by a shot.
Without bringing on further disaster,
Without abandoning your lion-hearted father—
If I were to leave your father behind,
“They will utterly destroy me,
Cut off his head and tie it up,
To the khagan of Beijing
Carry it away as a gift,” I thought.
With Akayar as my companion,
When your father drank the poison,
I fought time and again.
I made my white headscarf a banner.
Against Kokchokoz and Kozkaman
I raised a tumult time and again.
Though a woman, I made myself a warrior.
I carried your father away to safety;
Though a wife, I made myself his equal.
I hurried, beside myself with fear.
For my fierce lord there was no other way:
To Kaiypchy's mountain,
Into the very cave,
To a rocky pinnacle no raven could reach,
With mortal difficulty I took him and nursed him.
Your father wasted away, wounded;
Thus I endured hardship.
Though a woman, made myself a warrior:
Thus I nursed your father.
That poison given to your father
Had been left fermenting forty years.
It would corrode steel at a touch.
Let alone a person drinking it,
If it so much as touched his skin,
His gallbladder would burst within him.
From the city of Great Beijing
That poison had been specially sent.
From Karykan's presence it came:
“Let alone drinking it, that Burut
Will die if he merely smells it.
He will behold Judgment Day.
Even if he has protecting spirits,
Kozhosan Manas will die,” they said.
Carefully tended and prepared for that purpose,
Kozkaman brought it with him.
Weeping and pleading with his idol,
With the inside lined with rawhide,
He had the substance dried
And preserved it ceaselessly for forty years.
Your leopard father, the gray-maned hero—
He noted how unsuspecting he was.
“So that he keeps drinking,” he thought.
That Kalmyk, born to deceit,
Mixed it into liquor and shook it up.
Your father swallowed it and fell straight down.
Unable to speak, he collapsed face down.
Lest death overtake him,
I sought a remedy upon the earth.
I had Orolmo-Too searched
And healing medicinal herbs
Of a thousand kinds brought back.
Unable to collect my wits,
I sent a rider on Zhelmaian.
I wrote letters across the world.
Enteri, swift as a whirlwind,
I sent searching in Mekedilda.
From Egypt and Baghdad,
For the Green-Black medicine—
When he reached Medina,
Five spiritual masters there,
Friends of your valiant father,
Had found a solution.
In Baghdad, that vast treasury,
There was a green-black medicine.
Let me tell you about that medicine.
When Hindustan was raided,
When sixty mighty warriors died,
When the Khoja saw them dead,
He took them by the flank and cut them open.
The gall of those sixty mighty warriors
He took for medicine, they say.
He cut the vessels and attached a label,
